first_impression.reaction: Our daughter sent this with a note saying 'Mum, can you do your side?' The opening is plain and sensible: a gentle reminder, a personal follow-up, then a last call. No silly slang up top. I read it all on the iPad. It's useful to me because I'll be the one ringing the aunts and my mother's friends, and it actually says to split the list between families and to call older relatives. The short paragraphs are easy to read. My only real gap is that the destination wording forgets the guests I worry about most, the older ones who need help getting about.

journey.quote: Send a gentle reminder before your reply date, a personal follow-up once it has passed, and a last call only if a name is still blank.
journey.reaction: Clear and courteous. Three steps, not pestering. That's how I'd want it done.

journey.quote: Match the channel to the guest: a text for friends, an email or printed card for a formal suite, a call for older relatives.
journey.reaction: Thank you. Not everyone in our family is on their phone all day, and nobody made me feel old-fashioned for saying so.

journey.section: Who to remind and how to reach them
journey.quote: Split the list between families. Each partner, or each set of parents, takes their own side, so every reminder comes from a familiar voice.
journey.reaction: This is me. Good. But it doesn't say how I get the answers back to the kids so we're not keeping two lists.

journey.section: Who to remind and how to reach them
journey.quote: Guests overseas need a little more thought: check their time zone before you call, and use the channel they already reply to you on.
journey.reaction: Practical. My cousin in England would not thank me for a 3am call.

journey.section: Who to remind and how to reach them
journey.quote: A group text or a shared email list shows everyone's names and numbers, and names, addresses and phone numbers are all examples of personal information.
journey.reaction: Sensible and it points to the government site. A bit lawyerly in the next paragraph, but I'd rather they were careful.

journey.section: Wedding RSVP reminder text message wording
journey.quote: [Guest name]! Quick nudge from the two of us: your RSVP is the last piece of our puzzle. Reply by [reply date] at [RSVP web address] and we will save you a seat (and a glass).
journey.reaction: Fine for her friends, not for my side. I'll use the formal ones. At least they give you the choice.

journey.quote: Please let us know of any dietary or access needs at the same time.
journey.reaction: Good, access needs are mentioned. My mother uses a walking frame, so this matters.

journey.section: RSVP reminder cards for a formal invitation suite
journey.quote: If the card carries a QR code to your RSVP page, print the web address beside it.
journey.reaction: Yes. Half my friends won't scan those things, and they're right not to trust them.

journey.section: What to say when you call or see them in person
journey.quote: Keep it short, warm and specific, and have your guest list open so you can note the answer straight away.
journey.reaction: Useful script. I'll print it and keep it by the phone.

journey.section: Reminding guests for a destination wedding
journey.quote: Your answer helps us confirm numbers with our venue, and the travel and accommodation details are at [RSVP web address].
journey.reaction: This is the one that matters for an overseas wedding, and it's the one that doesn't ask about mobility or access. That's exactly what I'd need to know before Mum books a flight.

journey.section: Reminding guests for a destination wedding
journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor plans venue, travel, vendors and payments anywhere in the world, as one point of contact from start to finish, working in your time zone.
journey.reaction: One point of contact and they handle payments. That's who I'd want accountable. I'd still want to know their name and speak to them.

journey.section: Ready to plan the weekend around the replies
journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor is your single point of contact from start to finish, quotes in AUD and confirms inclusions in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: AUD and in writing before we commit. That's what I'd forward to Geoff.

unanswered_questions: Can I, as a parent paying part, join the first conversation with the Wedded Advisor, and is it a phone call with a real person? (deferred business detail)
Are deposits protected if an overseas supplier fails, and whose name is on the contract? (deferred business detail, not expected in an RSVP article)
Who do we ring if something goes wrong overseas after hours? (deferred business detail)

turn_offs_found.quote: This is your friendly reminder that a seat, a meal and a dance floor are waiting for your answer. Reply by [reply date] at [RSVP web address] and we will stop politely nagging.
turn_offs_found.why: A little too cute for my side of the family, but it's clearly labelled 'Light' and the formal version is right above it. Not a reason to leave.

would_share_with: My husband, the closing paragraph about AUD quotes and confirming inclusions in writing
My sister, who is helping with our side, the phone call script and the 'Split the list between families' paragraph
My daughter, the destination wording, with a note to add access needs

cta_reaction.quote: Your Wedded Advisor is your single point of contact from start to finish, quotes in AUD and confirms inclusions in writing before you commit.
cta_reaction.why: The right words: one person, AUD, in writing. But I came here to help with reminders, not to book anything. I'd pass it to my daughter and Geoff, and I'd only enquire after a phone call with a real person.

top_3_changes: Add mobility and access needs to the destination wedding reminder wording, so older guests are asked before they book travel. Suggested edit 1.
Tell parents and helpers who make calls to pass each answer back to the couple, so there is still only one list. Suggested edit 2.
Nothing else would stop me reading. The Light wording is a bit cute for older guests, but the formal versions are right beside it, so no change needed.

suggested_edits.old: > Dear [Guest names], we are so looking forward to welcoming you to [destination]. Could you let us know by [reply date] whether you will join us? Your answer helps us confirm numbers with our venue, and the travel and accommodation details are at [RSVP web address].
suggested_edits.new: > Dear [Guest names], we are so looking forward to welcoming you to [destination]. Could you let us know by [reply date] whether you will join us? Your answer helps us confirm numbers with our venue, and the travel and accommodation details are at [RSVP web address]. Please also tell us about any dietary, mobility or access needs so we can plan around them.
suggested_edits.why: Older relatives with a walking frame or other needs are the guests a parent worries about most on a destination wedding. The formal email already asks about access needs; the destination wording should too.

suggested_edits.old: Split the list between families. Each partner, or each set of parents, takes their own side, so every reminder comes from a familiar voice.
suggested_edits.new: Split the list between families. Each partner, or each set of parents, takes their own side, so every reminder comes from a familiar voice. Ask each helper to pass every answer back to you as it comes in, so your one guest list stays accurate.
suggested_edits.why: As the parent doing the ringing, I need to know how my answers get back to the couple. Ties into the 'keep one list' advice later in the article.

checks.check: Every journey point, turn-off and CTA reaction has an exact quote from the draft
Stayed in character as Margaret (funding parent): read top to bottom on iPad, focused on older relatives, her side of the list, accountability and a phone call
No invented brand facts; deposit protection, after-hours contact and parent involvement placed in unanswered_questions

Suggested edits are exact old/new strings and add no prices, statistics, day counts, platform or vendor names, fees, on-the-ground staff, room blocks, availability, or any suggestion the Advisor chases guests or handles RSVPs
VERIFY markers and HTML comments (fact tags, image slots, meta) ignored
No invented problems: only one medium objection raised; tone of Light wording noted as low and not requiring change

open_questions.question: Should the destination reminder wording ask about mobility and access needs (suggested edit 1)? It mirrors the access-needs line already in the formal email, so no new facts are needed.
Deposit protection, after-hours contact and whether a paying parent can join the first call are deferred business details; flag for the business rather than adding to this RSVP article.

assumptions: Margaret arrived via a link from her daughter asking her to help remind her side of the family, reading on an iPad.
Relevance is 4 because the article directly covers parents splitting the list and calling older relatives.
Likelihood to enquire is 2: an RSVP reminder article is not a reason for her to book a planner, though the closing lines on AUD and writing earn trust.
Husband's name (Geoff) and her mother's walking frame are character colour from the persona card and earlier panels, not page facts.
Fast mode: full article read top to bottom; FAQ skimmed as it repeats the body.
